hero.headline: SoFlo Market brings free Independence Day celebration to Boca Raton City Hall July 4
hero.teaser: The popular monthly market will feature a kids parade, DJ, vendors, food, and appearances by Boca Raton firefighters and police officers at the free holiday event.
hero.body:
Founder and organizer Tatiana Freitas is preparing the SoFlo Market to transform Boca Raton City Hall into a patriotic celebration hub this Fourth of July. The free event takes place Saturday, July 4, and will draw families, food lovers and local shopping enthusiasts throughout Palm Beach County. According to Freitas, the market's core mission centers on supporting small local businesses while bringing the community together. For the holiday edition, organizers are layering in extra patriotic touches that promise to make the celebration memorable.

The day's activities blend family entertainment with Independence Day spirit. Attendees can enjoy face painting, a foggy bubble station, mini golf and balloon twisting alongside the market's collection of handmade crafts and desserts. A kids' parade and DJ performances will keep the energy high, while the first 20 children through the gate receive a free gift. The SoFlo Market's flamboyant flamingo mascot will make a live appearance that organizers expect will be a crowd draw. Unique vendors and gourmet food options will round out the offerings throughout the afternoon.

Community partnerships strengthen the event's family-focused atmosphere. Boca Raton firefighters and police officers have been invited to participate and connect with residents. Kyle Freitas, Tatiana's son, and Eddie, her husband, serve as part of the organizing team coordinating the day's activities. Generators will provide on-site electricity for the event. Strong cell service will allow visitors to share their experiences instantly across social media, with behind-the-scenes coverage planned for the market's Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and YouTube channels.

The Independence Day market represents more than just shopping and entertainment. Independent markets like SoFlo play an increasingly important role in local economies by providing exposure for small businesses and creating gathering spaces where neighbors connect. By combining the market with Fourth of July traditions, organizers blend economic support with cultural celebration. Freitas emphasized the deeper purpose: "We want to make people proud to call this place home." While SoFlo Market operates monthly, Freitas notes that the Independence Day edition consistently stands out as a highlight. The event runs from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. at Boca Raton City Hall, located at 201 West Palmetto Park Road. Admission is free.

cards.headline: Florida enacts tighter property tax restrictions on local governments, November ballot fight ahead
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis signed new legislation this week that restricts how cities, counties and special districts can increase property tax revenue. The laws require local governments to stay closer to the rollback rate, which is set to generate roughly the same property tax revenue as the previous year, and mandate larger voter approval margins to exceed that rate. Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia emphasized that "we need government at all levels to start thinking about spending cuts," signaling the state's commitment to limiting revenue growth.

Those who support the new restrictions characterize them as essential protections for taxpayers and argue that local governments have allowed spending to grow too rapidly as property values increase. However, local officials express concern that the new constraints, when combined with a proposed constitutional amendment on the November ballot, could create significant shortfalls in city and county budgets. The amendment, designated as Amendment 3, would expand homestead exemptions on non-school property taxes, increasing the exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and then to $250,000 in 2028. Proponents argue this change would provide substantial relief to homeowners, while opponents worry that the tax savings some residents receive could result in service reductions, increased fees, or property tax increases in other areas.

The property tax debate has intensified with a new outside political campaign launching efforts to convince voters to reject the amendment. This campaign adds another significant element to what observers expect will be one of Florida's most closely watched and contentious ballot measures this autumn. The combination of the recently signed restrictions and the proposed amendment represents a major shift in how local governments throughout Florida, including those on the Treasure Coast, will be able to fund essential services moving forward.

These changes reflect a broader conservative push to limit government spending and property tax increases at the local level. As communities across the state prepare for November's election, the debate over how to balance taxpayer relief with adequate public funding remains a central issue. Local governments must now navigate stricter revenue requirements while anticipating additional limitations if voters approve Amendment 3.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested for holding teens at gunpoint after Orbeez prank
cards.teaser: Gregory Allen Davis, 49, and a 15-year-old were arrested Wednesday evening in Port St.
cards.body:
A 49-year-old man and a 15-year-old were arrested Wednesday evening in Port St. Lucie after an Orbeez prank escalated into an armed confrontation near SW Morelia Lane and SW Acapulco Terrace. Gregory Allen Davis and his fiancée called 911 after being shot at while driving, believing they were hit with a BB or pellet gun. While his fiancée remained on the phone with the dispatcher, Davis exited the vehicle armed with a 9mm handgun and ordered the teens to the ground at gunpoint. A witness captured video of the incident as Port St. Lucie police deployed their first responder drone.

Officers arrived moments later and discovered an Orbeez toy gun had been used. According to Port St. Lucie police, three teens told them they thought the vehicle belonged to a friend and shot at it with the Orbeez gun as part of a game. PSLPD determined Davis "had multiple opportunities to safely disengage while officers were actively responding." Davis was charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without intent to kill and false imprisonment of a child to commit aggravated abuse. The 15-year-old was charged with shooting or throwing a missile at or into an occupied vehicle. Police said the incident serves as a reminder that "Pranks involving Orbeez guns, airsoft guns, BB guns, or other toy firearms are not harmless. They can create fear, provoke dangerous reactions, and result in criminal charges."

cards.headline: DeSantis Signs Property Tax Restrictions as Amendment 3 Fight Intensifies Statewide
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis signed new legislation this week that restricts how cities, counties and special districts across Florida can raise property tax revenue. The laws align local governments more closely with the rollback rate, which is intended to generate approximately the same property tax revenue as the previous year, and mandate larger voter approval margins to exceed that threshold. Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia emphasized that governments at all levels should begin considering spending reductions to address budgetary concerns.

Advocates of the new restrictions frame them as taxpayer protections, arguing that local governments have allowed their budgets to expand too rapidly as property values have increased across the state. However, local officials have expressed concern that these new constraints, combined with a constitutional amendment scheduled for the November ballot, could create substantial shortfalls in city and county budgets. The restrictions will affect property tax revenue collection for the upcoming fiscal year across all Florida jurisdictions.

Amendment 3, which will appear on November ballots, would gradually expand homestead exemptions on non-school property taxes in two phases: raising the exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and then to $250,000 in 2028. Proponents contend the amendment would provide significant financial relief to homeowners. Critics, however, contend that the tax savings for some property owners could result in service reductions, increased fees, or tax increases in other areas. An outside campaign has recently launched urging voters to reject the amendment, adding intensity to what is expected to be one of Florida's most prominent ballot debates this fall.

The combination of DeSantis' newly signed property tax restrictions and the November constitutional amendment vote ensures that property tax policy will remain a central issue in Florida politics through the end of the year. Local governments across the state are now developing budget plans to operate under these new constraints while simultaneously tracking the amendment campaign that could further limit their available revenue sources.

cards.headline: 15-year-old St. Lucie County girl missing for three weeks
cards.teaser: Deputies are seeking tips on a 15-year-old girl who has been missing from St. Lucie County for three weeks.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is asking for the public's help in locating a 15-year-old girl who has been missing for three weeks. Deputies are actively seeking tips and information about her whereabouts.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the sheriff's office.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz closes as Everglades detention center empties, environmental fight continues
cards.teaser: The controversial Everglades immigration detention facility known as Alligator Alcatraz is now empty, but environmental advocates and the Miccosukee Tribe say the fight over the land is far from over.
cards.body:
Trailers are rolling out of the remote immigration detention center in the Everglades known as Alligator Alcatraz, but environmental advocates and members of the Miccosukee Tribe say the fight over the land is far from over. The facility is being dismantled piece by piece after holding undocumented immigrants. A group gathered at the entrance Friday morning, with many arguing that the closure alone does not undo the harm they believe was done to one of the most sensitive ecosystems in the country. Elise Bennett of the Center for Biological Diversity said the work is not finished until all infrastructure comes out. Betty Osceola of the Miccosukee Tribe echoed that sentiment, stating "it's not over for me until all that infrastructure comes out." Environmental advocates say high-intensity lighting, diesel generators, heavy paving and continuous traffic may have damaged critical habitat for endangered Florida panthers and other wildlife.

Eve Samples, executive director of Friends of the Everglades, called the facility an obscene waste of taxpayer dollars to the tune of about a billion dollars. The group has a pending federal lawsuit against the facility. A recent proposal from Miami-Dade County's mayor would transfer the roughly 25,000-acre space to the National Park Service for conservation. However, Osceola said her tribe has a deep and personal connection to the landscape and believes the Miccosukee people are its rightful stewards.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz detainees scattered to facilities across U.S. as legal battles grow more complex
cards.teaser: After the closure of the controversial detention facility in the Everglades, detainees have been sent to facilities in Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, and even Tacoma, Washington, creating new challenges for families and attorneys.
cards.body:
Immigration attorney Richard Hujber said detainees from Alligator Alcatraz have been scattered across the country following the facility's closure. According to Hujber, detainees have been sent to facilities in Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, and as far as Tacoma, Washington. He said one of his clients was moved all the way to Washington state.

The relocations create massive challenges when fighting for bonds and navigating immigration law. Hujber explained that different circuit courts in different parts of the country have different laws, and some circuits have denied bond requests. With bond now out of reach for some, detainees are left questioning whether they should keep pushing toward residency or asylum or give up and self-deport. Gov. Ron DeSantis says roughly 21,000 people have been deported from the facility since it opened nearly a year ago. Anna Maria Hernandez's cousin was released just before Alligator Alcatraz shut down and is now under an order of supervision, which allows him to drive, work and live in the U.S. The Baker County facility in North Florida remains operational.

cards.headline: Republican governor's race intensifies with ad spending but no debates scheduled before primary
cards.teaser: U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds remains the only Republican candidate meeting the party's debate criteria, leaving rivals Paul Renner, Lt. Gov. Jay Collins and James Fishback continuing to argue voters deserve a head-to-head contest before ballots are cast.
cards.body:
With Florida's Aug. 18 primary creeping closer, the Republican race for governor kept intensifying this week, though still not on a debate stage. U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds remains the only Republican candidate meeting the party's debate criteria, leaving rivals Paul Renner, Lt. Jay Collins and James Fishback continuing to argue voters deserve a head-to-head contest before ballots are cast. Renner criticized the debate process in a recent interview and suggested internal party politics are helping protect the frontrunner, saying what they're doing is really Byron Donalds' bidding. Donalds rebuffed the calls during a Florida Chamber press conference announcing their endorsement of his campaign, calling the governor's race a job interview and saying if he's applying for a job, it's not his responsibility to help his competitor get a job interview.

So far, no debate has materialized even from local news outlets, but the race is moving quickly elsewhere. Collins announced what his campaign called a multi-million dollar statewide advertising blitz, while Donalds is planning a $20 million statewide ad buy through the primary. Fishback tried to keep his insurgent campaign in the spotlight by naming former South Florida police officer and deputy campaign manager Sean Lozano as his running mate.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz detainees scattered across U.S. as legal battles continue after facility closes
cards.teaser: Immigration attorney Richard Hujber says detainees from the closed Everglades facility have been sent to facilities in Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico and even Tacoma, Washington, creating massive challenges for families and legal cases.
cards.body:
After the closure of the controversial Alligator Alcatraz detention facility in the Florida Everglades, detainees have been transferred to facilities across the country, creating significant legal complications for immigration cases. According to immigration attorney Richard Hujber, detainees have been sent to Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, and as far as Tacoma, Washington. These dispersals pose major challenges for those fighting for bonds and navigating immigration law, as different circuit courts across the country have varying legal standards. Hujber explained that different circuits have issued different rulings on bond eligibility, leaving some detainees unable to secure release while their cases proceed.

For detainees without access to bonds, the situation has become dire. Many now face the difficult choice of continuing to fight for residency or asylum status or pursuing self-deportation. Hujber noted that detainees question whether continued legal battles are worthwhile if bond is unattainable. Gov. Ron DeSantis reported that roughly 21,000 people have been deported from the facility since it opened nearly a year ago. Some families experienced relief when detainees were released before closure, such as Anna Maria Hernandez's cousin, who is now under an order of supervision allowing him to work, drive, and live in the U.S. The Baker County facility in North Florida remains operational.

cards.headline: John Morgan names new political party Common Ground Party, members to be called Grounders
cards.teaser: Orlando attorney John Morgan announced his new political party will be called the Common Ground Party, with the $100,000 prize money shared among more than 250 people who suggested the name.
cards.body:
Orlando attorney John Morgan announced this week that his new political party will be called the Common Ground Party, with members known as "Grounders." Morgan said it's worth a try to undo the gridlock, the hate, and all of the meanness that has fallen into politics on all sides, though he acknowledged uncertainty about whether the effort will succeed. The $100,000 contest to name the party will have its prize money shared among the more than 250 people who suggested "Common Ground Party."

Morgan has positioned the party as a home for voters frustrated with both Democrats and Republicans. However, significant questions remain unanswered: what the party's platform will be, whether it can secure ballot access, and whether the Grounders can become a legitimate political force or prove to be another short-lived third-party experiment in Florida politics.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce's Florida Highwaymen Museum featured in America 250 Road Trip for nation's 250th birthday
cards.teaser: The Florida Highwaymen Museum at 1234 Avenue D in Fort Pierce is a featured stop on the America 250 Road Trip celebrating the country's 250th birthday.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce announced this week on its Facebook page that the Florida Highwaymen Museum is a featured stop on the America 250 Road Trip, the nation's celebration of its 250th birthday. The museum, which opened this year, celebrates one of America's most iconic art movements through exhibitions featuring 26 Black artists who began painting in the 1950s. These artists created bold, colorful landscapes of Florida's untouched beauty and sold their work along the roadside when segregation prevented them from entering traditional galleries. Located at 1234 Avenue D, the museum is the nation's only one with exhibitions that include paintings from each of the 26 renowned Highwaymen artists.

The museum operates on a seasonal schedule. During summer from June 16 through July 31, it is open Saturday and Sunday from noon to 4 p.m. The museum will close in August and reopen in September with a new exhibit. Beginning September 1 through June 15, the museum will feature expanded hours of operation during fall and spring.

cards.headline: Donation sites across Palm Beach County collecting emergency supplies for Venezuela earthquake victims
cards.teaser: Four locations in Palm Beach County are accepting first aid kits, bandages, flashlights, batteries, solar phone chargers and other supplies to support those impacted by the earthquakes in Venezuela.
cards.body:
Several locations across Palm Beach County are accepting donations of emergency supplies to support those impacted by the earthquakes in Venezuela. The Guatemalan-Maya Center at 1776 Lake Worth Rd in Lake Worth Beach, Yoly's Venezuelan Food at 3090 S. Jog Road in Greenacres, Doña Arepa at 515 NE 20th St. in Boca Raton, and Rojas Law Office at 309 Lake Ave. in Lake Worth Beach are currently collecting donations.

Needed items include first aid kits, bandages, gauze, antiseptic wipes, pain-relief medications, flashlights, batteries, solar phone chargers and baby formula. The Global Empowerment Mission, a humanitarian group in Doral, activated its emergency response team Thursday and is preparing a shipment of food, water and hygiene products. Other ways to donate include the Emergency Relief for Venezuela Earthquake Victims and Support Earthquake Relief in Venezuela campaigns.

hero.headline: Former Alligator Alcatraz detainees scattered across U.S. as facility closes
hero.teaser: Detainees from the closed Everglades detention facility have been transferred to Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico and Washington state, creating new legal challenges.
hero.body:
The closure of the Alligator Alcatraz detention facility in the Florida Everglades has left detainees dispersed to immigration centers nationwide, creating significant obstacles for those fighting their cases. According to immigration attorney Richard Hujber, individuals have been transferred to facilities in Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, and Washington. "I had a client moved all the way to Tacoma, Washington, like it can't get farther than that," Hujber said. The geographic separation adds another layer of difficulty for families already struggling with the immigration process.

The scattering of detainees across different regions complicates legal representation and bond hearings. Hujber explained that immigration law varies significantly depending on location. "There's different laws in different circuit courts in different parts of the country," he said, noting that some courts have rejected bond requests that might have succeeded elsewhere. This inconsistency in rulings leaves detainees uncertain about their prospects for release. For many, the inability to secure bond raises larger questions about whether continuing to fight for residency or asylum status is worthwhile, with some considering self-deportation as their only option.

The facility's closure marks the end of nearly a year of operation. Governor Ron DeSantis reported that approximately 21,000 people were deported from the facility during its time in operation. However, not all detainees faced deportation. Anna Maria Hernandez's cousin was released just before the facility shut down and now lives under an order of supervision, which permits him to work, drive, and reside in the United States. Hernandez expressed her relief at her cousin's release while acknowledging the emotional toll the detention had taken on their family. "We lived every day wondering if our family is safe," she said, urging others not to endure similar suffering.

The future remains uncertain for many former detainees and their families. Hujber emphasized that while families want to continue fighting their cases, the burden ultimately falls on the detainees themselves to pursue their legal options. The Baker County facility in North Florida continues operating, but for those transferred from Alligator Alcatraz, the path forward is unclear. The closure has left hundreds of individuals separated from family support systems and navigating an immigration system with inconsistent standards, raising questions about fairness and access to justice across different regions of the country.

cards.headline: Martin County woman sentenced to 29 years for killing cyclist on 10-Cent Bridge
cards.teaser: Elise Elder, 25, received just over 29 years in prison for the June 2024 death of Martin Drummond, a well-known Stuart publisher and community member.
cards.body:
Elise Elder, 25, was sentenced Friday to just over 29 years in prison for killing 67-year-old Martin Drummond on the 10-Cent Bridge in June 2024. Elder received 17 years for fleeing the scene and just over 12 years for DUI manslaughter, to be served consecutively for a total of 29 years and one-and-a-half months. She was also given one year probation and her license was revoked for life. Florida Highway Patrol said Drummond was riding his bike east on A1A toward South Sewall's Point Road in the bike lane at approximately 6:45 a.m. when Elder's 2019 BMW 535I went into the bike lane and rear-ended the bicyclist. She then fled the scene and was arrested at her residence. Investigators said Elder was driving drunk from Daytona Beach and was over the legal limit at the time of her arrest.

Drummond was a well-known member of the Stuart community, the publisher of a local magazine, and known as a mentor and spiritual leader. During sentencing, Elder told the court, "I want to be accountable to myself and everyone in this room. I destroyed a family and life of an innocent human being, and I'm so sorry and regretful of that." Lori Drummond, Martin's wife, told the court she forgives Elder, saying "If he could come back, he would say to Elise Elder, that he's forgiven her, even as have I."

hero.headline: West Boca Raton homeowner faces repeated delays on My Safe Florida Home grant despite completed work
hero.body:
Anne Bendel of West Boca Raton has encountered multiple obstacles in her attempt to receive a state grant designed to help homeowners strengthen their homes against storms. The persistent delays have tested her patience as she navigates the My Safe Florida Home program, which typically awards grants up to $10,000 to eligible homeowners.

Bendel first reached out to WPTV in May regarding her application, which was being delayed due to missing paperwork from her insurance company. After resolving that initial issue, representatives with My Safe Florida Home informed her in May that her application status was complete. However, just one week later, the program requested additional documentation, specifically a permit of completion for a large impact window that Bendel had installed. She promptly provided the requested document, but new questions then arose about dates on her paperwork. Her application has since been sent back for further review, leaving the status of her grant funding uncertain. She paid $8,000 out of pocket for the home improvements and is hoping to recover some of those costs through the grant.

The My Safe Florida Home program has been instrumental in assisting thousands of homeowners throughout Florida by providing financial support for storm-resistant upgrades and helping them qualify for insurance discounts. However, Bendel's experience has undermined her confidence in the program's reliability. She described the process as particularly challenging because she lacks access to a computer and must handle all communications through her phone without assistance from others. "It's gut-wrenching," she said about managing the application process under these constraints. Despite completing all her required work, obtaining necessary permits, and securing the insurance coverage the program asked for, Bendel believes the program continues to introduce new requirements. She expressed frustration about what she perceives as unfair treatment, suggesting the program may be creating additional obstacles once homeowners have already finished their projects.

WPTV contacted the Florida Department of Financial Services in Tallahassee to inquire about Bendel's case and the current status of her grant application. Bendel, who describes herself as persistent and thorough, maintains that she has fulfilled every requirement presented to her. Her situation highlights potential challenges within the grant application process that may warrant further examination by state officials overseeing the program.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Haitians at risk of deportation after Supreme Court eliminates Temporary Protected Status
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County, home to 68,400 Haitian immigrants, faces upheaval after the Supreme Court sided with the Trump administration to eliminate Temporary Protected Status for thousands from Haiti and Syria.
cards.body:
The Supreme Court has sided with President Donald Trump's administration in eliminating Temporary Protected Status for thousands of people from Haiti and Syria, leaving hundreds of thousands at risk of deportation, including many in South Florida. Temporary Protected Status allows foreign citizens already in the United States to stay, work, and raise their families while their home countries deal with turmoil from natural disasters, political unrest, or violence. According to the Migration Policy Institute, Florida has the largest Haitian immigrant population in the United States, with Palm Beach County ranking third statewide and nationally at 68,400 Haitians, behind Broward County with 86,100 and Miami-Dade County with 78,800.

Stecko Dulcio, who has operated a Haitian restaurant in Riviera Beach for five and a half years, expressed alarm about the decision. Dulcio, a U.S. citizen, stated that gangs have taken over Haiti, claiming houses, controlling transportation, and fueling violence. Attorney Byrnes Guillaume, who is Haitian and represents many people losing TPS status, explained that elimination means people have no legal standing, can no longer work, and must go into the shadows. The ruling impacts roughly 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians nationwide. Since January of last year, the Department of Homeland Security has ended protections for people from more than 13 countries.

cards.headline: Former Haitian national team players mentor youth soccer players in Boca Raton
cards.teaser: Former members of the Haitian national soccer team spent time in Boca Raton this week mentoring the next generation of players at the L'Union Fait La Force Training Center.
cards.body:
Former members of the Haitian national soccer team are mentoring youth players through L'Union Fait La Force, a premier soccer development program based at a training center in Boca Raton. The program is hosting a clinic from June 25-28 teaching top-level Haitian soccer players the sport's fundamentals. Former team captain Jean-Marc Alexandre, an Atlantic High School and Lynn University graduate who was a member of Real Salt Lake's 2009 MLS Cup-winning team, said the camp's purpose is to give children a pathway to the youth national team since they are not living in Haiti.

For young players like Nohe Chevry and Luis Etienne, the clinic represents significant opportunity. Chevry moved to Palm Beach County with his family in 2022 from Haiti due to safety concerns as unrest grew. He joined L'Union Fait La Force after arriving in the area, drawn by the chance to learn from former professional players who have navigated pro contracts and national team experience. Etienne said the clinic offers potential exposure for the national team. Chevry's ambitions extend beyond the clinic, stating his goal is to play in the World Cup and win it.

cards.headline: SoFlo Market brings patriotic celebration to Boca Raton City Hall on July 4
cards.teaser: The popular SoFlo Market will turn Boca Raton City Hall into a hub of red, white and blue celebration on Independence Day with a kids parade, DJ, unique vendors and gourmet food.
cards.body:
The SoFlo Market will transform Boca Raton City Hall into a patriotic celebration on Saturday, July 4, drawing families, food lovers and local shopping enthusiasts from across Palm Beach County. Founder and organizer Tatiana Freitas said the market's mission is to uplift small local businesses and bring the community together. For the holiday, organizers are adding extra patriotic elements, including a kids' parade, a DJ, unique vendors, gourmet food and free gifts for the first 20 children through the gate.

Visitors can expect face painting, a foggy bubble station, mini golf, balloon twisting, handmade crafts and desserts. A live appearance by the SoFlo Market's flamingo mascot is set to be a crowd favorite. Boca Raton firefighters and police officers have been invited to share the day with residents. Kyle, Freitas's son, and Eddie, her husband, are part of the organizing team. The event will be held at 201 West Palmetto Park Road from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Admission is free. Freitas said the Independence Day edition is always a standout, and emphasized the goal: "We want to make people proud to call this place home."

cards.headline: West Palm Beach veteran says Hanley Center helped him recover from eight years of drug addiction
cards.teaser: Chris Claflin, a Navy pilot and Harvard Business School graduate, said the Hanley Center in West Palm Beach changed everything for the better after eight years of drug addiction.
cards.body:
Chris Claflin, a Navy pilot who flew jets in combat and graduated from Harvard Business School, struggled with drug addiction for eight years. He traced the onset of his addiction, in part, to not dealing with trauma he experienced as a child. After more than a year of sobriety, Claflin has a message for anyone struggling, especially veterans: "You can't do this on your own. It's not something you can figure out. Once you get so far down the rabbit hole, you can't pull yourself out on your own."

The care Claflin received at the Hanley Center in West Palm Beach changed everything for the better. He is now working to become a certified counselor after receiving help at the facility. Ahead of the July Fourth holiday, WPTV is examining ways to celebrate and support the military, highlighting the Hanley Center as a valuable resource for service members and others struggling with mental health and well-being.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce Florida Highwaymen Museum featured on America 250 Road Trip
hero.teaser: The Florida Highwaymen Museum in Fort Pierce has been selected as a featured stop on the America 250 Road Trip celebrating the nation's 250th birthday.
hero.body:
The city of Fort Pierce announced on its Facebook page this week that the Florida Highwaymen Museum is a featured stop on the America 250 Road Trip. The museum, located at 1234 Avenue D, opened this year and celebrates 26 Black artists who began painting in the 1950s.

The Highwaymen created bold, colorful landscapes of Florida's untouched beauty and sold them along the roadside when segregation kept them out of traditional galleries. The Fort Pierce museum is the nation's only one with exhibitions that include paintings from each of the 26 renowned Highwaymen artists.

The museum is currently operating on summer hours, open Saturday and Sunday from noon to 4 p.m. from June 16 through July 31. The museum will be closed in August and reopen in September with a new exhibit. Fall and spring hours from September 1 through June 15 will be expanded.

cards.headline: Fort Myers walks off on St. Lucie Mets with home run in Friday night game
cards.teaser: The Fort Myers Mighty Mussels defeated the St. Lucie Mets with a walk-off home run by Young in their Friday matchup.
cards.body:
Young hit a walk-off home run to lift the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels over the St. Lucie Mets on Friday night. The blast ended the game in dramatic fashion and gave Fort Myers the victory.

The walk-off homer capped what had been a competitive game between the two Florida State League clubs. Young's heroics sent the Mighty Mussels home with a win over the visiting St. Lucie squad.

The St. Lucie Mets will look to regroup after the tough defeat. The team plays its home games in Port St. Lucie as part of the New York Mets minor league system.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Mets fall 6-2 to Fort Myers as Mighty Mussels hit 4 home runs
cards.teaser: The St.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie Mets lost 6-2 to the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels on Friday night as the visiting team slugged four home runs at the Mets' home ballpark. The Mighty Mussels' offensive barrage proved too much for the St. Lucie pitching staff to overcome in the Florida State League matchup.

The loss comes during a challenging stretch for the St. Lucie Mets as they continue their season in the minor league baseball circuit. The Mets gave up six runs while managing just two of their own against Fort Myers pitching.

The Mighty Mussels displayed power throughout the contest, with multiple players contributing to the four-homer attack. The St. Lucie Mets were unable to match the offensive production despite playing on their home field.

The teams will continue their series as the Mets look to bounce back from the defeat. The St. Lucie Mets are the Class A affiliate of the New York Mets organization and play their home games in Port St. Lucie.

cards.headline: Former Haitian national soccer team members mentor youth players in Boca Raton
cards.teaser: Former Haiti national team captain Jean-Marc Alexandre and other former national team players are hosting a soccer clinic in Boca Raton from June 25-28 for young Haitian players.
cards.body:
Former members of the Haitian national soccer team mentored young players in Boca Raton this week at the L'Union Fait La Force Training Center, just days after Haiti played Morocco on Wednesday night. The clinic runs from June 25-28 and teaches top-level Haitian soccer players including Nohe Chevry and Luis Etienne. Jean-Marc Alexandre, an Atlantic High School and Lynn University graduate and former Haiti national team captain, runs the premier soccer development program. Alexandre was a member of Real Salt Lake's 2009 MLS Cup-winning team. According to Alexandre, the program's purpose is to give young players a pathway to the youth national team since they are not living in Haiti.

Chevry moved to Palm Beach County from Haiti in 2022 with his family due to safety concerns. He said learning from former professional players who have navigated pro contracts is valuable. "It's a great opportunity to learn; they've been through all of the soccer stuff, pro contracts, so they can teach us, and it's really kind of them to do that," Chevry said. For Chevry, his ambitions extend beyond the clinic. "I will take this to a high level, and my goal is to play in the World Cup and probably win it," he said. Luis Etienne also expressed appreciation for the opportunity, saying it could provide exposure for the national team.

cards.headline: Boca Raton homeowner faces new delays on My Safe Florida Home grant despite completed work
cards.teaser: Anne Bendel of West Boca Raton says her My Safe Florida Home grant application keeps hitting hurdles even after she completed the required work and submitted all paperwork.
cards.body:
Anne Bendel of West Boca Raton first contacted WPTV in May about delays with her My Safe Florida Home grant application. Initially, paperwork from her insurance company held up her case, but that issue was eventually resolved. My Safe Florida Home then told Bendel in May that her status was complete. However, a week later, representatives asked for additional documents, including a permit of completion for a large impact window. After she provided the permit, the program raised questions about dates on the documents. Bendel's application is now back under review, leaving her hopes for grant money uncertain.

Bendel has spent $8,000 out of pocket on home improvements and says she completed all required work, obtained permits, and secured the insurance coverage requested by the program. The My Safe Florida Home program has helped thousands of homeowners across Florida with grants of up to $10,000 to fortify homes against storms and earn insurance discounts. WPTV has contacted the Florida Department of Financial Services in Tallahassee regarding Bendel's case and the status of her grant.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz detainees scattered across U.S. after facility closure
cards.teaser: Immigration attorney Richard Hujber says detainees from the closed Alligator Alcatraz facility in the Everglades have been moved to facilities in Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, and Washington state.
cards.body:
Detainees from Alligator Alcatraz, the controversial detention facility deep in the Florida Everglades, have been scattered across the country following the facility's closure. According to immigration attorney Richard Hujber, detainees have been sent to facilities in Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, and as far as Tacoma, Washington. The dispersal creates significant legal challenges, as Hujber explains that different circuit courts across the country have different laws regarding bond availability. In some circuits, bond is no longer available, forcing detainees to decide whether to continue fighting for residency or asylum or to self-deport. Governor Ron DeSantis reported that roughly 21,000 people have been deported from the facility since it opened nearly a year ago.

For some families, the closure brought relief. Anna Maria Hernandez's cousin was released just before Alligator Alcatraz shut down and is now under an order of supervision, which allows him to drive, work and live in the U.S. However, Hujber emphasizes that the fight remains difficult and depends on the detainees' own determination to continue. The Baker County facility in North Florida remains operational, leaving many former detainees and their families facing an uncertain future.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach veteran credits Hanley Center with helping him overcome 8-year drug addiction
cards.teaser: Chris Claflin, a Navy combat pilot and Harvard Business School graduate, said the Hanley Center in West Palm Beach helped him get sober after eight years of drug addiction.
cards.body:
Chris Claflin, a Navy pilot who flew jets in combat and graduated from Harvard Business School, said his success fell apart when he became drug addicted for eight years. Claflin is currently more than a year sober and credits the care he received at the Hanley Center in West Palm Beach with changing everything for the better.

Claflin traced the onset of his drug addiction, in part, back to not dealing with trauma he experienced as a child. He has a message for anyone struggling, especially veterans: you can't do this on your own, it's not something you can figure out, and once you get so far down the rabbit hole, you can't pull yourself out on your own. Claflin is now working to become a certified counselor after receiving help at the Hanley Center, which provides treatment for mental health and substance abuse issues for service members and others struggling with addiction.

hero.headline: SoFlo Market brings free Independence Day celebration to Boca Raton City Hall July 4
hero.teaser: The popular monthly market will feature a kids parade, DJ, vendors, food, and appearances by Boca Raton firefighters and police officers at the free holiday event.
hero.body:
Founder and organizer Tatiana Freitas is preparing the SoFlo Market to transform Boca Raton City Hall into a patriotic celebration hub this Fourth of July. The free event takes place Saturday, July 4, and will draw families, food lovers and local shopping enthusiasts throughout Palm Beach County. According to Freitas, the market's core mission centers on supporting small local businesses while bringing the community together. For the holiday edition, organizers are layering in extra patriotic touches that promise to make the celebration memorable.

The day's activities blend family entertainment with Independence Day spirit. Attendees can enjoy face painting, a foggy bubble station, mini golf and balloon twisting alongside the market's collection of handmade crafts and desserts. A kids' parade and DJ performances will keep the energy high, while the first 20 children through the gate receive a free gift. The SoFlo Market's flamboyant flamingo mascot will make a live appearance that organizers expect will be a crowd draw. Unique vendors and gourmet food options will round out the offerings throughout the afternoon.

Community partnerships strengthen the event's family-focused atmosphere. Boca Raton firefighters and police officers have been invited to participate and connect with residents. Kyle Freitas, Tatiana's son, and Eddie, her husband, serve as part of the organizing team coordinating the day's activities. Generators will provide on-site electricity for the event. Strong cell service will allow visitors to share their experiences instantly across social media, with behind-the-scenes coverage planned for the market's Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and YouTube channels.

The Independence Day market represents more than just shopping and entertainment. Independent markets like SoFlo play an increasingly important role in local economies by providing exposure for small businesses and creating gathering spaces where neighbors connect. By combining the market with Fourth of July traditions, organizers blend economic support with cultural celebration. Freitas emphasized the deeper purpose: "We want to make people proud to call this place home." While SoFlo Market operates monthly, Freitas notes that the Independence Day edition consistently stands out as a highlight. The event runs from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. at Boca Raton City Hall, located at 201 West Palmetto Park Road. Admission is free.

cards.headline: Florida Mango Festival showcases 75 vendors, rare varieties at West Palm Beach Convention Center today
cards.teaser: Florida-grown mangoes will take center stage Saturday, June 27, at the Florida Mango Festival inside the Palm Beach County Convention Center.
cards.body:
Florida-grown mangoes will take center stage Saturday, June 27, at the Florida Mango Festival inside the Palm Beach County Convention Center at 650 Okeechobee Boulevard in West Palm Beach. The event features more than 75 vendors serving local mango varieties, grafted trees, tropical fruits, and mango-themed products in an air-conditioned indoor venue. Festival co-organizer Vince Rogers previewed some of the state's most unique varieties, including Fruit Cocktail, a sweet multi-layered flavor; Orange Sherbet, offering creamy citrus notes; and Pineapple Pleasure, with tropical pineapple undertones. Rogers said Florida hosts more than 350 mango varieties, far beyond what is typically available in grocery stores.

Throughout the day, visitors can attend educational talks on home mango growing and grafting techniques led by Alex Salazar of Tropical Acres Farms, who will offer tips for both beginners and seasoned growers. Additional features include an ID Your Mango booth, a scion exchange for online mango community members, and a master display of Florida's diverse mango cultivars. First pick ticket holders can enter at 9 a.m., with general admission beginning at 10:30 a.m. Garage parking is included with tickets, with limited availability. Paid public parking is available nearby north of Okeechobee Boulevard. Tickets and more information are available at floridamangofestival.com.

cards.headline: George Snow Scholarship Fund in Boca Raton awards record $7.5 million to 470 students
cards.teaser: The nonprofit has now distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students, making it the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County.
cards.body:
The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, awarded more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026, according to President Tim Snow. Founded over 40 years ago, the nonprofit has distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students, making it the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County. The program bridges the gap between traditional financial aid and what students and families can afford by offering four-year commitments to ensure stability throughout college.

Vice President of Development Jay Brandt said GSSF's services extend beyond financial help, providing mentorship, professional development, and resources like the College Compass podcast. One 2026 recipient, Zya Chow, earned both the Royal Palm Hearing Aid Scholarship and the Davidowitz Family Caregiving Youth Scholarship. Chow, a Wellington Community High School graduate, plans to attend Georgetown University. The fund also operates the Doyle-Whelchel Scholars Boutique, led by Scholar Services Coordinator Garvey Antoine, which offers professional, formal, and casual wear so scholars can step into interviews, internships, and campus life with confidence.

cards.headline: Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League urges South Florida residents to prepare pets for hurricane season
cards.teaser: The shelter recommends microchipping, creating emergency kits with three days of supplies, and conducting storm drills with pets in designated safe rooms.
cards.body:
Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League is urging South Florida residents to create a disaster plan for their pets before the next hurricane hits. Dr. Alyssa Comroe, CEO of Peggy Adams, told WPTV that the safest place for pets during a hurricane is alongside their owners. The shelter's expert team recommends several key steps to protect pets during Florida's hurricane season, which runs from June through November.

Pet owners should ensure their animals wear a collar with current identification and have an updated microchip registered with correct contact information. Owners should introduce pets to a designated safe room, such as a walk-in closet or downstairs bathroom, and conduct practice runs beforehand. Pet owners should prepare an emergency kit containing a three-day supply of food and water in airtight containers, bowls, a sturdy carrier, bedding, towels, medications for two weeks, vaccination records, first-aid supplies, litter and box for cats, leashes, harnesses, cool packs, wipes, waste bags, and multiple forms of visible ID. The organization also recommends keeping a printed list of local pet-friendly shelters and hotels in an accessible place and maintaining recent photos of pets, ideally with their owner, to help with identification if separated. Conducting hurricane drills that include pets' daily routines inside the safe room can maximize their comfort during an actual storm.

hero.headline: DeSantis Signs Property Tax Restrictions as Amendment 3 Fight Intensifies Statewide
hero.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis signed new legislation this week that restricts how cities, counties and special districts across Florida can raise property tax revenue. The laws align local governments more closely with the rollback rate, which is intended to generate approximately the same property tax revenue as the previous year, and mandate larger voter approval margins to exceed that threshold. Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia emphasized that governments at all levels should begin considering spending reductions to address budgetary concerns.

Advocates of the new restrictions frame them as taxpayer protections, arguing that local governments have allowed their budgets to expand too rapidly as property values have increased across the state. However, local officials have expressed concern that these new constraints, combined with a constitutional amendment scheduled for the November ballot, could create substantial shortfalls in city and county budgets. The restrictions will affect property tax revenue collection for the upcoming fiscal year across all Florida jurisdictions.

Amendment 3, which will appear on November ballots, would gradually expand homestead exemptions on non-school property taxes in two phases: raising the exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and then to $250,000 in 2028. Proponents contend the amendment would provide significant financial relief to homeowners. Critics, however, contend that the tax savings for some property owners could result in service reductions, increased fees, or tax increases in other areas. An outside campaign has recently launched urging voters to reject the amendment, adding intensity to what is expected to be one of Florida's most prominent ballot debates this fall.

The combination of DeSantis' newly signed property tax restrictions and the November constitutional amendment vote ensures that property tax policy will remain a central issue in Florida politics through the end of the year. Local governments across the state are now developing budget plans to operate under these new constraints while simultaneously tracking the amendment campaign that could further limit their available revenue sources.

cards.headline: DeSantis Closes Everglades Immigration Detention Facility After Nearly 21,000 Deportations
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis announced the Everglades immigration detention facility known as 'Alligator Alcatraz' is now empty after facilitating nearly 21,000 deportations in almost a year of operation.
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis announced Thursday that the Everglades immigration detention facility, nicknamed "Alligator Alcatraz," is now empty after operating for nearly a year. DeSantis said the facility served its purpose as an emergency expansion of immigration detention capacity and that the mission made Florida safer. The closure marks the end of active operations at the controversial project, which became one of the most contentious initiatives of his second term.

However, the shutdown does not resolve ongoing disputes surrounding the facility. Critics continue raising concerns about the cost, detainee treatment, hurricane safety, and environmental damage. Environmental groups have argued the state failed to properly account for impacts on the Everglades and Big Cypress region. DeSantis stated he expects the federal government to reimburse Florida for the project's price tag, which has climbed into the hundreds of millions of dollars. The reimbursement request remains pending, meaning the facility's closure marks the end of its operations but not the end of political and legal disputes over its existence.

cards.headline: Republican Governor's Race Intensifies as Byron Donalds Refuses Debate While Rivals Push for Forum
cards.teaser: U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds remains the only Republican candidate meeting the party's debate criteria for the governor's race, while rivals Paul Renner, Lt. Gov. Jay Collins and James Fishback argue voters deserve a head-to-head contest before the Aug. 18 primary.
cards.body:
With Florida's Aug. 18 primary approaching, the Republican gubernatorial race intensified this week without materializing on a debate stage. U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds remains the only Republican candidate meeting the party's debate criteria, prompting rivals Paul Renner, Lt. Jay Collins and James Fishback to continue calling for a head-to-head contest. Renner criticized the debate process in a recent interview, suggesting internal party politics are protecting the frontrunner. "What they're doing, really, is Byron Donalds' bidding," Renner said. Donalds has rebuffed the calls, most recently during a Florida Chamber press conference announcing their endorsement of his campaign. He characterized the governor's race as a job interview, saying "If I'm applying for a job, it's not my responsibility to help my competitor get a job interview."

Despite the absence of debates, the race accelerated through advertising and campaign announcements. Collins announced a "multi-million dollar statewide" advertising blitz, while Donalds is planning a $20 million statewide ad buy through the primary. Fishback named former South Florida police officer Sean Lozano as his running mate and deputy campaign manager. Lozano stated at the Tallahassee announcement: "We will not politely manage Florida's decline. We will stop it."

cards.headline: Orlando Attorney John Morgan Names New Florida Political Party 'Common Ground Party'
cards.teaser: Orlando attorney John Morgan announced his new political party will be called the Common Ground Party, with members known as Grounders, after a $100,000 contest drew more than 250 submissions.
cards.body:
Orlando attorney John Morgan announced this week that his new political party will be called the Common Ground Party, with members known as "Grounders." The $100,000 naming contest drew more than 250 suggestions, and the prize money will be shared among those who proposed the winning name. Morgan said the effort is worth attempting to undo the gridlock, hate, and meanness that has fallen into politics on all sides, though he acknowledged uncertainty about whether it will succeed.

Morgan has pitched the Common Ground Party as a home for voters frustrated with both Democrats and Republicans. However, major questions remain unanswered: what the party's platform will be, whether it can secure ballot access, and whether the Grounders can become a legitimate political force or simply another short-lived third-party experiment in Florida politics.

cards.headline: Florida Pavilion Opens at Great American State Fair in Washington Through July 10
cards.teaser: The Florida Pavilion joins exhibits from every state and six U.S. territories at the expo on the National Mall, showcasing Florida's history, wildlife, agriculture and tourism through five signature experiences.
cards.body:
The Florida Pavilion opened Thursday at the Great American State Fair on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., and will remain open through July 10. The pavilion joins exhibits from all 50 states and six U.S. territories at the expo, hosted by Freedom 250. Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a statement that as the nation celebrates 250 years of independence, Florida is proud to showcase the culture and history that has helped shape America. The exhibit begins in St. Augustine, the nation's oldest continuously inhabited European-established city, where Florida's story starts with Juan Ponce de León's arrival in 1513.

Visitors can explore five signature experiences: Florida's History Heritage, The Manatee: Florida's Iconic Marine Mammal, Florida's Natural Resources, Fresh From Florida: Florida's Agricultural Heritage, and Live More Floridays celebrating Florida tourism. VISIT FLORIDA President and CEO Bryan Griffin said the pavilion will let visitors explore Florida's long history, natural treasures, and current landmarks. The fair is open Sunday through Wednesday from 10 a.m. and Thursday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 11 p.m., with extended hours until midnight on July 4. Food and beverages will be available for purchase throughout the fairgrounds, and clear bags are required for entry.

cards.headline: South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn Endorses Kendrick Meek Jr. in Florida's 24th Congressional District Race
cards.teaser: Civil rights icon and longtime Democratic power broker Jim Clyburn is backing Kendrick Meek Jr. in his campaign for CD 24, citing Meek's work with the Human Rights Campaign, the ACLU, SAVE and communities across Florida.
cards.body:
U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina is endorsing Kendrick Meek Jr. in Florida's 24th Congressional District race, citing Meek's work as an attorney and civil rights advocate with organizations including the Human Rights Campaign and the American Civil Liberties Union. Clyburn said Meek understands the stakes because he has been active in the fight for voting rights and equality. Clyburn noted that Republicans across the South are working to weaken Black political power and erase Black representation in Congress, including in his own district. He called Meek the kind of leader House Democrats need to win back the majority, stand up to Donald Trump and MAGA Republicans, and move the country forward.

Meek carries significant family ties to the seat. His grandmother, Carrie Meek, was among Florida's first Black members of Congress since Reconstruction, and his father, Kendrick Meek, served the district from 2003 to 2011. Meek is one of seven Democrats running in CD 24, which covers Miami Gardens in Miami-Dade County and Hollywood, Miramar, and Pembroke Park in Broward County. Other candidates include Miami-Dade Commissioner Oliver Gilbert, state Sen. Shevrin Jones, physician-veteran Rudy Moise, and former County Commissioner Jean Monestime. With more than 68.7% of voters backing Kamala Harris in 2024, the Democratic Primary on August 18 will effectively determine who succeeds the retiring U.S. Rep. Frederica Wilson.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds Raises Nearly $700,000 in Week While GOP Gubernatorial Opponents Struggle with Fundraising
cards.teaser: Gubernatorial front-runner Byron Donalds added nearly $253,000 to his campaign account and another $435,000 to his PAC in the week ending June 19, continuing to dominate fundraising in the GOP race with nearly $66 million on hand.
cards.body:
With more than 50 days remaining before the Aug. 18 primary, Byron Donalds continued to dominate fundraising in the Republican gubernatorial race. In the week ending June 19, Donalds raised nearly $253,000 to his campaign account and $435,000 to his Friends of Byron Donalds PAC, bringing his total money on hand to nearly $66 million. However, his total will decrease on the next report due to a $20 million media buy already booked.

Despite the substantial spending ahead, Donalds is outpacing his three main opponents who have struggled to gain traction with donors. James Fishback raised $4,825 to his campaign account and nothing to his Florida First PAC, with roughly $117,000 total to spend as of June 19. Jay Collins raised just over $11,000 to his campaign account and $1,500 to his political committee, leaving him with roughly $3.5 million to spend. Former House Speaker Paul Renner raised less than $30,000 to his campaign account for the second consecutive fundraising period and $13,000 to his PAC, with roughly $2.5 million to spend as of June 19. No candidates will debate at Saturday's GOP event, with Donalds and allies asserting that his opponents are not viable.

hero.headline: OnPoint Mobile Injections launches shockwave therapy for knee pain in Stuart
hero.teaser: A Stuart medical service has introduced advanced shockwave therapy for knee pain relief.
hero.body:
OnPoint Mobile Injections has launched advanced shockwave therapy for knee pain relief in Stuart. The service is now available in the area.

The treatment represents a new option for residents dealing with knee pain. OnPoint Mobile Injections provides mobile medical services in Stuart.

cards.headline: Martin County woman sentenced to 29 years in prison for 10-Cent Bridge cyclist death
cards.teaser: Elise Elder, 25, was sentenced Friday to just over 29 years in prison for killing 67-year-old Martin Drummond in a June 2024 crash on the 10-Cent Bridge.
cards.body:
Elise Elder, 25, was sentenced Friday to just over 29 years in prison for the death of 67-year-old Martin Drummond in a June 2024 crash on the 10-Cent Bridge. Elder received 17 years for fleeing the scene and just over 12 years for DUI manslaughter, to be served consecutively, totaling 29 years and one-and-a-half months. She was also given one year probation and her driver's license was revoked for life. According to Florida Highway Patrol, Drummond was riding his bike east on A1A toward South Sewall's Point Road in the bike lane at approximately 6:45 a.m. when Elder's 2019 BMW 535I went into the bike lane and rear-ended the bicyclist. She then fled the scene and was arrested at her residence. Investigators said Elder was driving drunk from Daytona Beach and was over the legal limit at the time of her arrest.

Drummond, a well-known member of the Stuart community, was the publisher of a local magazine and known as a mentor and spiritual leader. Elder took the stand to express her remorse, stating "I want to be accountable to myself and everyone in this room. I destroyed a family and life of an innocent human being, and I'm so sorry and regretful of that." Drummond's daughter Jessica Cornett described the ongoing impact on her family, noting her children sleep in his clothes and her 7-year-old still cries for his papa when scared. His wife, Lori Drummond, told the court she forgives Elder, saying Martin would have forgiven her as well.

cards.headline: Multi-vehicle crash on NW Federal Highway in Stuart causes traffic delays
cards.teaser: A crash involving multiple vehicles on NW Federal Highway in Stuart caused traffic delays Friday.
cards.body:
Multiple vehicles were involved in a crash on NW Federal Highway in Stuart on Friday. The incident caused traffic delays in the area.

The crash occurred on NW Federal Highway in Stuart. Motorists experienced delays as a result of the incident.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Florida Highwaymen Museum featured in America 250 Road Trip
cards.teaser: The Florida Highwaymen Museum in Fort Pierce has been selected as a featured stop on the America 250 Road Trip celebrating the nation's 250th birthday.
cards.body:
The Florida Highwaymen Museum, which opened this year in Fort Pierce, is a featured stop on the America 250 Road Trip, celebrating the nation's 250th birthday. The city announced the designation this week on its Facebook page. Located at 1234 Avenue D, the museum is the nation's only one with exhibitions that include paintings from each of the 26 renowned Highwaymen artists.

The museum celebrates 26 Black artists who began painting in the 1950s, creating bold, colorful landscapes of Florida's untouched beauty and selling them along the roadside when segregation kept them out of traditional galleries. Summer hours run from June 16 through July 31, with the museum open Saturday and Sunday from noon to 4 p.m. The museum will be closed in August and reopen in September, featuring a new exhibit. Fall and spring hours beginning September 1 through June 15 will be expanded.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County locations collecting supplies for Venezuela earthquake victims
cards.teaser: Several locations across Palm Beach County are accepting donations of emergency supplies to support those impacted by the earthquakes in Venezuela.
cards.body:
Several locations across Palm Beach County are accepting donations of emergency supplies for those affected by earthquakes in Venezuela. The Guatemalan-Maya Center at 1776 Lake Worth Road in Lake Worth Beach, Yoly's Venezuelan Food at 3090 S. Jog Road in Greenacres, Doña Arepa at 515 NE 20th Street in Boca Raton, and Rojas Law Office at 309 Lake Avenue in Lake Worth Beach are currently collecting donations. Needed items include first aid kits, bandages, gauze, antiseptic wipes, pain-relief medications, flashlights, batteries, solar phone chargers and baby formula.

A humanitarian group in Doral is also supporting relief efforts. Volunteers with the Global Empowerment Mission activated its emergency response team Thursday and are preparing a shipment of food, water and hygiene products for victims. Those interested in additional donation options can contribute through the Emergency Relief for Venezuela Earthquake Victims and Support Earthquake Relief in Venezuela.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz detainees scattered across U.S. as legal battles continue after facility closure
cards.teaser: Detainees from the closed Alligator Alcatraz facility have been moved to locations across the country as immigration cases continue.
cards.body:
Immigration attorney Richard Hujber said detainees from the now-closed Everglades facility have been scattered to detention facilities in Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, and as far as Tacoma, Washington. "I had a client moved all the way to Tacoma, Washington, like it can't get farther than that," Hujber said. The dispersal creates significant legal challenges for immigrants fighting for bonds and navigating the immigration system. "There's different laws in different circuit courts in different parts of the country," Hujber explained. "And in different circuits and in different parts of this country they have said no." Some detainees now face the difficult choice of continuing to fight their cases or self-deporting, questioning whether pushing toward residency or asylum is feasible if they cannot secure bond.

Gov. Ron DeSantis reported that roughly 21,000 people were deported from the facility since it opened nearly a year ago. For some families, the closure brought relief. Anna Maria Hernandez's cousin was released just before the facility shut down and is now under an order of supervision, allowing him to drive, work and live in the U.S. However, Hujber emphasized the fight remains difficult and ultimately depends on the detainees themselves. The Baker County facility in North Florida continues to operate.

cards.headline: Environmental groups say Alligator Alcatraz closure doesn't undo Everglades damage
cards.teaser: Trailers are rolling out of the immigration detention center known as Alligator Alcatraz, but environmental advocates say the fight over the land continues.
cards.body:
Environmental advocates and members of the Miccosukee Tribe gathered at the entrance of the remote Everglades immigration detention center known as Alligator Alcatraz on Friday morning as the facility is being dismantled. Betty Osceola of the Miccosukee Tribe said the closure alone does not complete the work needed. "It's not over for me until all that infrastructure comes out," Osceola said. Elise Bennett of the Center for Biological Diversity said high-intensity lighting, diesel generators, heavy paving and continuous traffic may have damaged critical habitat for endangered Florida panthers and other wildlife. "All of this was subjected to immense damage. That harm has not been undone by the announcement of a closure," Bennett said.

Eve Samples, executive director of Friends of the Everglades, called the facility a misuse of public funds and natural resources. "It was an obscene waste of taxpayer dollars, dollars to the tune of about a billion dollars. It was an abuse of the Everglades," Samples said. A recent proposal from Miami-Dade County's mayor would transfer the roughly 25,000-acre space to the National Park Service for conservation. However, Osceola said she does not trust government agencies to protect the land and believes the Miccosukee people are its rightful stewards. "We are the best stewards to receive that landscape," Osceola said.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce's Florida Highwaymen Museum featured in America 250 Road Trip
hero.body:
A museum that opened this year in Fort Pierce is part of the festivities celebrating the country's 250th birthday. The city announced on its Facebook page this week that the Florida Highwaymen Museum is a featured stop on the America 250 Road Trip.

The museum celebrates 26 Black artists who began painting in the 1950s, creating bold, colorful landscapes of Florida's untouched beauty and selling them along the roadside when segregation kept them out of traditional galleries. Located at 1234 Avenue D, the museum is the nation's only one with exhibitions that include paintings from each of the 26 renowned Highwaymen artists.

The museum operates on a summer schedule from June 16 through July 31, opening Saturday and Sunday from noon to 4 p.m. Fall and spring hours from September 1 through June 15 will be expanded.

The museum will be closed in August and reopen in September, featuring a new exhibit.

hero.headline: Immigration Detainees from Alligator Alcatraz Scattered Across U.S. as Legal Battles Continue
hero.teaser: After the closure of Alligator Alcatraz, detainees have been sent to facilities across the country, creating massive challenges for families and attorneys navigating immigration law.
hero.body:
The closure of the controversial Alligator Alcatraz detention facility in the Florida Everglades has created a new crisis for immigrants who were not deported before the facility shut down. According to immigration attorney Richard Hujber, the detainees have been transferred to facilities across the country, including Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, and as far away as Tacoma, Washington. These dispersals have made it significantly harder for detainees and their legal representatives to navigate the immigration system effectively. Hujber explained that "there's different laws in different circuit courts in different parts of the country," meaning that strategies that work in one jurisdiction may not succeed in another.

The geographical separation of detainees from their legal representatives has created serious obstacles in their cases. Many detainees now face impossible choices about whether to continue fighting for residency or asylum status or to give up and return to their home countries voluntarily. With bond becoming unattainable for some due to the complications caused by transfers, detainees are caught in a difficult position. As Hujber put it, many are asking themselves whether they should "continue to fight this case, because if I can't even get a bond, what's the chance I'm going to get a green card or asylum?" The uncertainty has left families anxious about their loved ones' futures.

For some, however, the facility's closure brought relief. Anna Maria Hernandez's cousin was released just before Alligator Alcatraz permanently closed its doors. He is now under an order of supervision, which permits him to work, drive, and live in the United States. Hernandez has become an advocate for other families still facing detention, urging the government to allow others the same opportunity her cousin received. She reflected on the emotional toll of her family's experience, saying "we lived every day wondering if our family is safe." Her cousin's release represents the kind of outcome that other detainees and their families are hoping to achieve.

Despite the closure of Alligator Alcatraz, the fight for many detainees is far from over. The Baker County facility in North Florida remains operational, and uncertainty continues to cloud the futures of former detainees scattered across the country. Governor Ron DeSantis reported that approximately 21,000 people were deported from Alligator Alcatraz during its operation. Hujber emphasized that while families want to continue fighting for their relatives' cases, ultimately the decision rests with the detainees themselves. For many, this means navigating a complicated legal system from thousands of miles away from their support networks, with limited access to consistent legal representation.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz Closes as Environmental Fight Over Everglades Land Continues
cards.teaser: Trailers are rolling out of the remote immigration detention center in the Everglades known as Alligator Alcatraz, but environmental advocates and members of the Miccosukee Tribe say the fight over the land is far from over.
cards.body:
The immigration detention center known as Alligator Alcatraz is being dismantled, but environmental advocates and the Miccosukee Tribe say the fight over the roughly 25,000-acre Everglades site is far from over. A group gathered at the entrance Friday morning as trailers rolled out. Elise Bennett of the Center for Biological Diversity said the closure was gratifying but wished it was happening quicker. Betty Osceola of the Miccosukee Tribe said the work remains unfinished until all infrastructure is removed.

Environmental advocates say high-intensity lighting, diesel generators, heavy paving and continuous traffic may have damaged critical habitat for endangered Florida panthers and other wildlife. Eve Samples, executive director of Friends of the Everglades, called the facility an obscene waste of about a billion taxpayer dollars and an abuse of the Everglades. The group has a pending federal lawsuit against the facility. A recent proposal from Miami-Dade County's mayor would transfer the land to the National Park Service for conservation. However, Osceola said her tribe has a deep and personal connection to the landscape and believes the Miccosukee people are its rightful stewards, expressing distrust in federal and state government protection of the land.

cards.headline: West Boca Raton Homeowner Says My Safe Florida Home Grant Keeps Hitting Hurdles Despite Completed Work
cards.teaser: A West Boca Raton homeowner says her efforts to receive a promised grant from the state to fix up her home keep facing one hurdle after another.
cards.body:
Anne Bendel, a West Boca Raton homeowner, says her application for a My Safe Florida Home grant has faced repeated obstacles despite completing all required work. She first contacted WPTV in May regarding paperwork delays from her insurance company. After that issue was resolved, My Safe Florida Home notified her in May that her status was complete. However, a week later, representatives requested a permit of completion for a large impact window. After she provided it, questions arose about dates, and her application returned to review status.

Bendel paid $8,000 out of pocket for the work and said she completed all tasks, obtained permits, and secured insurance as required. "Everything is done, but it seems like when everything is done they find some other little task to send you," she said. The My Safe Florida Home program provides grants of up to $10,000 to thousands of homeowners across the state to fortify homes against storms and earn insurance discounts. WPTV has contacted the Florida Department of Financial Services in Tallahassee regarding Bendel's case and the status of her grant.
